stem: The two regression lines of a bivariate data set are 6x + 10y = 130 and 10x + 6y = 110. Using the appropriate regression line, what is the best estimate of y when x = 8?

per_option_rationale.rationale: To estimate y from a known x you must use the y-on-x line. Test the assignment: if 6x + 10y = 130 is y-on-x then b_yx = -6/10 = -0.6, and 10x + 6y = 110 as x-on-y gives b_xy = -6/10 = -0.6; their product 0.36 is at most 1, so this assignment is valid (the reverse gives 2.78 and is rejected). The y-on-x line is y = 13 - 0.6x, so at x = 8, y = 13 - 0.6*8 = 8.2.
Uses the x-on-y line 10x + 6y = 110 to predict y, giving y = (110 - 80)/6 = 5.0. That line is built to predict x from y and minimises horizontal errors; predicting y requires the y-on-x line instead.
Reports the mean ybar = 10, found from the intersection of the two lines, ignoring that x = 8 differs from xbar = 5 and that the slope then moves the estimate off the mean.
Drops the negative sign of the slope, using y = 13 + 0.6x to get 13 + 4.8 = 17.8. Both regression coefficients here are negative, so the y-on-x slope is -0.6, not +0.6.

explanation: Estimating y from x demands the y-on-x line, so first identify it. Taking 6x + 10y = 130 as y-on-x gives b_yx = -0.6 and 10x + 6y = 110 as x-on-y gives b_xy = -0.6, product 0.36 at most 1, so the assignment is admissible. The y-on-x line is y = 13 - 0.6x; at x = 8 the estimate is 13 - 4.8 = 8.2.

explanation_sections.punchline: Which line you use is the whole question: to predict y you need y-on-x, never x-on-y. The admissibility test tells you which is which.
explanation_sections.approach: When asked to estimate y from x, select the regression line of y on x by checking that the chosen coefficient pairing has product at most 1, write that line in the form y = a + b*x, and substitute the given x.
explanation_sections.lesson: Predict y from the y-on-x line and x from the x-on-y line; the two lines are not interchangeable for prediction.
explanation_sections.timing: About 175 seconds. The fastest elimination is 5.0, which comes from feeding x into the wrong line, the x-on-y line.
